claims.text: The activity, selectivity, and durability of Pt-based nanoscale catalysts during ethanol oxidation are governed by the balance between formation and removal of surface-adsorbed intermediates.
Transient adsorption of species such as CO and acetaldehyde at certain potentials enables ethanol oxidation to progress optimally.
Persistent accumulation of adsorbed intermediates poisons the catalyst and diminishes catalytic performance.
The investigated initial state consists of Pt-based nanoscale catalysts on conductive substrates with pristine surfaces characterized under inert conditions.
Potential steps between 0.2 and 1.0 V versus RHE will alter the formation and desorption of adsorbed ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Potential-dependent vibrational signatures measured by in situ FTIR reveal the formation and desorption of surface intermediates.
Timely adsorption and removal of intermediates limits catalyst poisoning.
Limiting poisoning promotes complete 12-electron oxidation of ethanol.
CO buildup interferes with the catalytic cycle and reduces activity.
At higher potentials, the CO adsorption band should decrease while current density increases.
Prolonged, high-intensity signals from poisoning intermediates should be associated with reduced catalytic performance.
The proposed mechanism applies at moderate ethanol concentrations and between 0.2 and 1.0 V versus RHE.
Very high ethanol concentration, unusual pH, or substantially different temperatures may change adsorption and desorption dynamics and invalidate the mechanism.
Introducing a CO scavenger should change the intermediate adsorption profile in the direction predicted by reduced CO poisoning.
The mechanism is falsified if intermediate bands do not change with potential in correlation with catalytic performance.
The mechanism is falsified if a persistent CO signal occurs without an associated decline in catalytic performance.
